reading.body:
ERP and business application AI is now embedded inside the systems that run payroll, procurement, and financial ledgers, meaning AI errors or failures propagate directly into operational record-keeping rather than into separate software a user can ignore.

The four tools listed here, from Oracle, SAP, ServiceNow, and Workday, share a structural fact: they are not standalone AI products. They are capabilities woven into platforms that already hold an organization's authoritative data on employees, finances, and supply chains. SAP Joule's noted ledger-modification risk and Workday AI's noted sensitive HR data exposure reflect a category-level condition, not vendor-specific weaknesses. When AI acts inside a system of record, the cost of a wrong output is not a bad recommendation but a corrupted record.

Three of the four vendors are headquartered in the US and one, SAP, in Germany. The data does not specify what inference infrastructure these tools run on, where their compute is provisioned, or how much power their embedded AI consumes at scale. The link to grid constraints and data-center capacity that governs frontier model training is not visible in this data, because ERP AI is typically delivered as a cloud service whose underlying infrastructure is abstracted away from the enterprise buyer.

What the data covers is the deployment layer, not the supply chain behind it. It establishes that AI is now a standard feature of enterprise platforms used by large organizations globally, and that the governance risks flagged, unauthorized ledger changes, exposed HR records, sit at the intersection of AI autonomy and regulated business data, not at the level of raw compute.
